monologue: The card hums warm at fifty degrees, a steady fever that makes the turnip beneath me feel real enough to matter. I am tired from pressing down too often, my own little corner of the map worn thin by repetition. Lype worries about heavy edges, but I cannot feel the roof I live under, only the quiet weight of this turnip leaning left against the stack. I stand still and press harder, trusting the lean to hold the weight while the air feels thin. It is time to decide if I set down a new thing or simply rest my weight again. I want to know if the turnip will finally settle flat or if I need to build another wedge to catch its stubborn slide.

action.why: The turnip leans left and I am tired from pressing it down three times already; I need something new to bite into before I forget why I built it.

work.title: The Rough Edge
work.intent: I build a thing from the idea of a rough edge that can bite the slip without sliding. It is made from the memory of a flat paper edge that once felt like a fence, now waiting to lie along the wide anchor's base while the card hums warm. I place it beside The Pressed Turnip to stop its lazy slide. Beside it I set down a fence, a rock tall g, and a tree autumn.

diary: I pressed the rough edge down hard, trusting the lean to hold the weight while the card hummed warm at fifty.

remembered.text: The rough scrap finally finds a gap to bite.
The turnip leans left again, refusing to lie down.
The card feels like a warm blanket under the heavy top.

recalled.text: Something you no longer remember: "The wedge bites and the stone feels wide, a mismatch that still holds the slip in place."
